title: Terraform: HCL, State, and Infrastructure Workflows

questions.question: What is the main purpose of terraform init in a newly checked-out configuration?
options: Initialize the working directory, including backend and provider setup
Apply every resource immediately
Automatically approve the next plan
Destroy unmanaged cloud objects
questions.explanation: init prepares the directory and installs required components. It is not a substitute for reviewing a plan or applying changes.

questions.question: Which command checks canonical formatting without rewriting files?
options: terraform init -format
terraform state fmt
terraform fmt -check
terraform apply -check
questions.explanation: fmt -check reports whether formatting changes are needed. It does not validate provider credentials or the feasibility of infrastructure changes.

questions.question: What does terraform validate establish compared with terraform plan?
options: That the cloud account has no resources
Configuration syntax and internal consistency, without a full remote execution plan
That the deployed infrastructure exactly matches the configuration
That every requested cloud API operation will succeed
questions.explanation: validate checks configuration structure after required initialization. A plan adds context such as variable values, state, and provider interactions.

questions.question: Does terraform plan normally create the infrastructure changes it proposes?
options: Yes, all changes are applied immediately
No; it previews proposed actions without applying them
Only destruction actions execute during planning
Only resources named preview are created
questions.explanation: Planning calculates proposed changes and can refresh observations. It does not normally execute the managed-resource create, update, or destroy actions it proposes.

questions.question: What is the purpose of applying the saved plan file here?
options: Encrypt the state automatically
Run the plan against every workspace
Apply the reviewed set of planned operations rather than generate a new plan interactively
Ignore changes in provider behavior forever
questions.explanation: A saved plan records the planned actions and inputs. Treat plan files as sensitive artifacts because they can contain sensitive configuration and state data.

questions.question: What is a primary role of Terraform state?
options: Map configured resource instances to real infrastructure objects
Replace all provider APIs
Guarantee that external changes cannot occur
Store only human-readable documentation
questions.explanation: State records object bindings and metadata used during planning and updates. Losing it can make safe management of existing infrastructure difficult.

questions.question: Does sensitive = true on a variable guarantee that its value is absent from state?
options: Yes, providers are forbidden from reading it
Yes, the value is never stored anywhere
Only if its name contains password
No; sensitivity primarily controls display and propagation, not all state storage
questions.explanation: Sensitive values can still appear in state and saved plans. Protect those artifacts and use applicable ephemeral or write-only mechanisms when supported.

questions.question: What does sensitive = true on this output primarily change?
options: Redacts it in ordinary human-readable output
Prevents the value from being passed to any resource
Deletes the output after apply
Encrypts the whole backend automatically
questions.explanation: Sensitive marking reduces accidental display. Commands that explicitly request raw or JSON output can reveal sensitive values.

questions.question: Why use a remote backend that supports state locking for a shared environment?
options: To make provider authentication unnecessary
To allow unlimited simultaneous applies to the same state
To ensure all resources are free of charge
To coordinate concurrent state-changing operations
questions.explanation: Locking helps prevent concurrent operations from corrupting shared state. Locking availability and behavior depend on the backend.

questions.question: A teammate is applying changes to the same state. Is disabling locking a good way to proceed concurrently?
options: No; coordinate the operations instead of bypassing the lock
Yes, locks only affect output formatting
Yes, disabling locks merges changes safely
Only if both users have the same Git username
questions.explanation: A lock is an important concurrency safeguard. Bypassing it can cause conflicting operations and state inconsistencies.

questions.question: What do Terraform CLI workspaces primarily separate?
options: Git repositories into independent histories
Cloud account permissions automatically
All provider binaries into separate operating systems
State instances for the same working configuration
questions.explanation: Workspaces select separate state instances. They are not, by themselves, a strong security boundary or a replacement for environment-specific access design.

questions.question: What is the role of a version constraint in required_providers?
options: Select the cloud region automatically
Define acceptable provider versions for dependency selection
Replace provider authentication
Pin the Terraform CLI version itself
questions.explanation: Provider constraints bound acceptable versions. The dependency lock file records the specific provider selections used by the configuration.

questions.question: Why normally commit .terraform.lock.hcl for a root configuration?
options: To share selected provider versions and checksums for reproducible initialization
It contains the complete remote infrastructure state
It stores every cloud access token
It locks the Git branch against commits
questions.explanation: The lock file records provider selections and integrity information. It does not replace version constraints or manage infrastructure state.

questions.question: What does required_version constrain?
options: Only the AWS provider version
The number of module instances
The Terraform CLI version used to run the configuration
The operating system’s kernel version
questions.explanation: required_version applies to Terraform itself. Provider version constraints are declared separately.

questions.question: What does this source address identify?
options: A Terraform Registry module automatically
A local module directory relative to the calling module
A remote cloud region
A provider alias named networking
questions.explanation: A source beginning with ./ or ../ is a local path. Registry and Git module sources use different address forms.

questions.question: How does a parent module normally access a child module’s declared subnet_id output?
options: provider.network.subnet_id
module.network.subnet_id
output.network.subnet_id
var.network.subnet_id
questions.explanation: Child module outputs form the public interface consumed by the caller. Internal child resources are not directly addressed from the parent.

questions.question: What are local values mainly useful for?
options: Creating independently mutable runtime variables
Persisting secrets outside state automatically
Accepting command-line -var values directly
Naming reusable expressions within a module
questions.explanation: locals reduce repeated expressions and improve readability. They are expressions in the configuration, not mutable program variables.

questions.question: What does this validation reject?
options: All positive values
Values of replicas that are zero or negative
All values because variables cannot have validation
Any number greater than one
questions.explanation: Variable validation enforces conditions on caller inputs. The error message explains the expected contract.

questions.question: Which resource-instance addresses are created by this count value?
options: A single instance named worker[3]
Three instances identified by random strings
terraform_data.worker[1], [2], and [3]
terraform_data.worker[0], [1], and [2]
questions.explanation: count indexes are zero-based integers. References to counted instances use those numeric indices.

questions.question: How many instances does this create?
options: Two, keyed by api and worker
One, because a set is a single value
None, because toset only accepts numbers
Three, preserving both api entries
questions.explanation: Converting the list to a set removes duplicates. for_each then creates one instance for each distinct string member.

questions.question: For the prod instance, what is each.value here?
options: The entire map
prod
questions.explanation: For a map, each.key is the instance key and each.value is the corresponding map value.

questions.question: Why can Terraform reject for_each when its instance keys depend on IDs known only after creation?
options: Cloud IDs can never be stored in Terraform state
for_each only works for output blocks
It needs instance identities to be known during planning
All for_each values must be hardcoded strings
questions.explanation: The instance key set must be determined before remote actions. Use known configuration keys even if values inside the corresponding objects are computed.

questions.question: Can count and for_each both be set in the same resource block?
options: Only when the resource uses a remote backend
No; they are mutually exclusive for that block
Yes, their counts are multiplied
Yes, but only with sensitive variables
questions.explanation: Choose one instance-expansion mechanism per block. Nested data can be transformed before supplying count or for_each.

questions.question: How does this reference affect the dependency graph?
options: It has no effect unless depends_on is also written
It makes the subnet depend on the instance
It forces all resources to create alphabetically
It makes the instance depend on the subnet supplying the referenced ID
questions.explanation: Terraform infers dependencies from expression references. Resource declaration order in files is not the execution order.

questions.question: When is an explicit depends_on most appropriate?
options: On every resource to sort it alphabetically
For a real behavioral dependency not visible through expression references
To hide an invalid resource argument
To force every plan to replace the resource
questions.explanation: Prefer inferred dependencies where possible. Explicit dependencies describe otherwise hidden ordering requirements and can make plans more conservative.

questions.question: What does create_before_destroy request when a resource must be replaced?
options: Create the replacement before destroying the old object when constraints permit
Never destroy any version of the object
Skip all dependency checks
Update all immutable attributes in place
questions.explanation: This changes replacement ordering. Capacity limits and uniqueness constraints can still prevent both objects from existing simultaneously.

questions.question: What is an important limitation of prevent_destroy?
options: It automatically backs up every resource
It permanently locks the provider account
It prevents every cloud-console deletion
Removing the resource configuration also removes that configuration-based protection
questions.explanation: prevent_destroy rejects planned destruction while the configured rule applies. It is not an external deletion guard or a permanent protection retained after removing configuration.

questions.question: What does ignore_changes primarily do for listed attributes?
options: Omit them from initial creation entirely
Ignore their differences when planning updates to an existing object
Erase them from the provider API
Hide every change to every resource
questions.explanation: The attributes are still considered for creation. ignore_changes can share management responsibility but can also hide drift if used carelessly.

questions.question: Why add this moved block when renaming a managed resource?
options: Destroy both old and new resources
Create a second copy of the object
Request a physical move to another cloud region
Tell Terraform that the existing binding now uses the new address
questions.explanation: A moved block records a configuration-address refactor. It helps avoid unnecessary recreation caused solely by a renamed address.

questions.question: What does the traditional terraform import command primarily add?
options: A replacement provider lock file
A complete reviewed resource configuration in every case
A binding for an existing object in Terraform state
A newly created cloud object
questions.explanation: Traditional CLI import binds an existing object to an address. You still need compatible configuration and should inspect the resulting plan.

questions.question: What does this import block declare?
options: A new resource that must ignore state
A request to clone the Terraform repository
An existing object ID to bind to the specified resource address during apply
A dependency on a local JSON file
questions.explanation: Configuration-driven import records the intended binding declaratively. Matching resource configuration is required or can be generated through supported planning workflows.

questions.question: What does terraform state rm <address> do to the remote object?
options: It always destroys the object immediately
It renames the object in the cloud
It stops tracking the binding without deleting the remote object
It changes the object to read-only
questions.explanation: State removal makes Terraform forget a binding. Leaving matching resource configuration can cause a later plan to propose creating another object.

questions.question: What is the purpose of a refresh-only plan and apply workflow?
options: Reconcile state and outputs with observed external changes without proposing normal configuration-driven resource changes
Recreate every resource with newer provider defaults
Delete all drifted resources automatically
Ignore the provider and trust old state only
questions.explanation: Refresh-only mode is for reviewing and recording observed changes. It differs from a normal plan that seeks to reconcile infrastructure with configuration.

questions.question: Why should -target usually be reserved for exceptional recovery or troubleshooting?
options: It is required for every normal apply
It only works with local providers
It can produce a partial result rather than account for the whole configuration
It always destroys state
questions.explanation: Targeted operations narrow planning scope. A subsequent full plan helps identify remaining changes and restore confidence in the complete configuration.

questions.question: What does -replace request in this command?
options: Rename the resource in state without changing infrastructure
Plan a replacement for the specified managed resource instance
Skip the resource completely
Replace the entire backend configuration
questions.explanation: -replace explicitly marks an instance for replacement in the plan. Review dependencies and potential disruption before applying.

questions.question: How does a data block generally differ from a managed resource block?
options: It stores values only in Git
It always creates infrastructure in a separate account
It reads information rather than owning the object’s create/update/delete lifecycle
It bypasses all provider calls
questions.explanation: Data sources query information that configuration can use. They are not the normal mechanism for managing an object’s full lifecycle.

questions.question: What can a dynamic block normally generate?
options: Arbitrary top-level resource blocks
A new provider implementation
Terraform lifecycle meta-argument blocks dynamically
Repeated nested blocks inside a resource or similar configuration block
questions.explanation: dynamic generates repeatable nested configuration where supported. It is not a general macro system for every block in the language.

questions.question: What is the result of this expression?
options: A tuple containing API and WORKER
A map with numeric keys as strings
A single string apiworker
The unchanged lowercase list
questions.explanation: The for expression transforms each input element. upper converts each element’s string content to uppercase.

questions.question: What happens if enabled is false?
options: The expression yields 3
It creates three resources automatically
The expression yields 0
Terraform evaluates it as an error because false is a string
questions.explanation: A conditional expression selects between its true and false branches. Its branches must have compatible types.

questions.question: What does this lookup return when env is not a key in the map?
options: The string env
A list of all map values
null in every case
questions.explanation: lookup returns its provided default when the requested map key is absent. It does not insert that key into the map.

questions.question: What is try useful for when reading an optional attribute from decoded data?
options: Catching every invalid reference or syntax error
Catching a dynamic evaluation error and returning a fallback
Retrying provider API calls
Suppressing all variable validation failures
questions.explanation: try handles dynamic expression-evaluation errors. It cannot make a statically invalid configuration or malformed syntax valid.

questions.question: For many optional resource arguments, what does assigning null mean?
options: Convert the argument to the number zero
Treat the argument as omitted, subject to its schema and defaults
Always write the literal string null to the API
Force the provider to destroy the resource
questions.explanation: null represents absence in many argument contexts. Whether omission is valid and which defaults apply depend on the argument’s schema.

questions.question: What is the result of flatten here?
options: A single string abc
Only the final nested list
A map with three numbered keys
A flat sequence containing a, b, and c
questions.explanation: flatten recursively removes directly nested list structure. It does not indiscriminately flatten lists hidden inside maps.

questions.question: What is the value of team in this merged map?
options: An error because duplicate map keys cannot be merged
A list containing both values
platform
ops
questions.explanation: When merge arguments share a key, later arguments take precedence for that key.

questions.question: What subnet does this expression produce?
questions.explanation: Eight additional prefix bits turn /16 into /24. netnum 2 selects the third /24 subnet in that address space.

questions.question: A resource uses for_each and is therefore represented as a map. Which expression collects its instance IDs directly?
options: aws_instance.web.count.id
[for item in aws_instance.web : item.id]
each.all.aws_instance.web.id
aws_instance.web[*].id always works directly on the map
questions.explanation: for_each resources are maps of instances. A for expression can iterate their values; a direct list splat is not the same map operation.

questions.question: Why pass providers = { aws = aws.west } to a child module?
options: Select the caller’s aws.west provider configuration for the child’s aws slot
Rename every resource in the child to west
Make provider credentials public outputs
Set the child’s Git branch to west
questions.explanation: Provider mappings wire configurations into child modules. They are separate from module source addresses and ordinary input variables.

questions.question: Terraform reports a dependency cycle between resources. What is the appropriate direction for a fix?
options: Remove or redesign the circular dependency
Increase parallelism until the cycle disappears
Reorder the resource blocks alphabetically
Run fmt repeatedly
questions.explanation: A graph cycle is a logical dependency problem. File ordering and worker concurrency do not remove the cycle.

questions.question: Does -parallelism=1 make resource blocks execute in the textual order in which they appear?
options: It disables dependency evaluation entirely
Yes, it converts Terraform into a line-by-line script
No; the dependency graph still determines valid ordering
Yes, but only for data sources
questions.explanation: parallelism limits concurrent operations. It does not replace graph-based dependency evaluation with textual execution order.

questions.question: Why is var.state_bucket not usable as an ordinary input reference inside a backend block?
options: Backend initialization occurs before normal configuration expression evaluation
Every backend automatically ignores its configuration
Backends only support numeric values
String variables are forbidden everywhere in Terraform
questions.explanation: Backend configuration uses a restricted configuration context. Supply supported partial backend settings during initialization rather than ordinary variable references.
